evidence.text: Remove all Prisma Optimize examples (#8514)
* Remove all Prisma Optimize examples
Prisma Optimize is being discontinued. This removes the entire
optimize/ directory (6 example projects) and the corresponding
section from the root README.
* Fix CI flaky tests by giving each dev server a unique name
The concurrent tests all called startPrismaDevServer() with the default
name "default" in stateless mode. On slow CI runners, multiple tests
would scan for servers simultaneously, find none, and all try to bind
the same port (51216), causing EADDRINUSE failures.
Passing a unique name per test lets the port allocator see other
servers and pick distinct ports.
* Fix EADDRINUSE by assigning explicit unique ports per test
The previous approach of using unique names didn't work because
stateless mode never writes server state to disk, so concurrent
tests still race on the same default port range.
Instead, assign each test its own set of 3 ports (server, database,
shadow database) from a counter starting at 52000. Since all tests
in a file share a single Node.js event loop, the synchronous counter
increment is atomic against concurrent async calls.
* Fix CI EADDRINUSE: use singleFork and unique ports per test
With singleFork: false, vitest distributes concurrent tests across
separate worker processes. Each worker re-imports the module, resetting
the port counter, so multiple workers race on the same ports.
Setting singleFork: true ensures all tests in a file share one process,
making the portOffset counter effective. Combined with explicit unique
ports per test (starting at 52000, 3 ports each), concurrent tests
never collide.
* Add debug logging for port assignment in CI
* Fix CI: run tests sequentially to avoid @prisma/dev port conflicts
@prisma/dev internally allocates ports beyond the 3 user-configurable
ones (port, databasePort, shadowDatabasePort). When many PGLite
instances start concurrently, they race on these internal ports
(51216+), causing EADDRINUSE.
Run tests sequentially (maxConcurrency: 1, remove describe.concurrent)
to ensure only one @prisma/dev server runs at a time. This is slower
(~4min vs ~1min per test file) but eliminates the flaky port conflicts
that have been failing CI consistently.

Live-verified 2026-08-07: 1080p h264 + aac, ~170s for a 3s clip. **Fixed in v12.295 — we had been sending a field that does not exist.** From v12.272 we passed `size: '9:16'`; the upstream has **no `size` parameter at all**, and it silently ignores fields it does not recognise, so every clip came back in the default 16:9. (A deliberately bogus `size` still returns HTTP 200 and creates a task — that is how the silent-fallback was proven.) Per Alibaba's own [HappyHorse text-to-video reference](https://help.aliyun.com/zh/model-studio/happyhorse-text-to-video-api-reference), the real fields are `ratio` (`16:9` default, `9:16`, `1:1`, `4:3`, `3:4`, `4:5`, `5:4`, `9:21`, `21:9`), `resolution` (`480P`/`720P`/`1080P`), `duration`, `watermark` and `seed`. The `usage` block the API returns — `{"SR": 1080, "ratio": "16:9"}` — is simply an echo of those two, which had been in plain sight all along. **Also fixed:** `watermark` defaults to **true** upstream, so every HappyHorse clip carried a bottom-right "Happy Horse" watermark; it is now off by default (`HAPPYHORSE_WATERMARK=1` restores it). Vertical is no longer gated off, but every finished task still cross-checks `usage.ratio`, and a mismatch disables that ratio for the rest of the run instead of burning shot after shot. - **Windows installs failed mid-`npm install` when VS Build Tools were absent** (#439) — `hnswlib-node@^3.0.0` ships no prebuilt binaries and runs `node-gyp rebuild` on every install; without the C++ toolchain installed the whole `agentic-qe` install crashed. Moved to `optionalDependencies` so npm tolerates the compile failure and continues; `HnswAdapter` already routes around a missing native binary at runtime via the pure-JS `ProgressiveHnswBackend`. Replaced the top-level static `import hnswlib from 'hnswlib-node'` in `src/integrations/embeddings/index/HNSWIndex.ts` with a lazy require so the package itself loads even when the native module is absent. README and the preinstall script document the toolchain requirement and disclose the brute-force degradation mode honestly.

- **RVF pattern store crashed every time the .rvf file already existed** (Jordi RUFLO P020) — `getSharedRvfAdapter` and the `pattern-store` factory always called `RvfDatabase.create()`, which throws `RVF error 0x0303: FsyncFailed` when the target file exists. Earlier init phases legitimately produce `patterns.rvf`, so every subsequent CLI / MCP boot crashed RVF init and silently fell back to SQLite (`hnswStats.nativeAvailable: false`). Reproduced and confirmed against both `@ruvector/rvf-node@0.1.7` and `0.1.8` — not a version regression. Replaced with a race-tolerant open-or-create ladder (try open → fall back to create → retry open on create-race) plus `dim()` verification after open so a dimension-mismatched file is detected and the caller degrades rather than corrupting silently.

- **`findUntestedFunctions` and `findImpactedTests` always returned empty** (Jordi RUFLO P220 follow-up) — both queries filter on `type='test'` source nodes joined to `type='covers'` edges, but `buildFromIndexResult` only ever wrote `type='file'` nodes and `imports` / `contains` edges. Added `HypergraphEngine.synthesizeTestCoverage()`, called from the coordinator after `buildFromIndexResult` succeeds, that re-tags test-shaped file nodes (`*.test.ts`, `*.spec.ts`, `_test.go`, etc.) as `type='test'` and writes `covers` edges from each test file to the function entities in the source files it imports. End-to-end verified on a fresh project: `aqe hg untested` correctly excludes covered functions; `aqe hg impacted src/calc.ts` returns the right test file.

- **Background workers registered but never ticked** — `src/mcp/entry.ts:211` overrode `getDaemon({ autoStart: false })`, neutering `workerManager.startAll()`. The "[MCP] Background workers started (11 workers)" log read total *registered* workers, not *scheduled* ones, so dream cycles, pattern promotion, and learning consolidation never ran on schedule. Now uses the canonical default (`DEFAULT_CONFIG.autoStart = true` per `workers/daemon.ts:53`); see ADR-001 "AQE workers WAL contention strategy".

- **HNSW vector index loaded empty under our default unified-bridge path** — `PatternStore.initializeHNSWInternal()` had the embedding-load loop only in the legacy fallback branch. With `useUnifiedHnsw: true` (our default per ADR-071), the function returned at the unified-bridge branch *before* the load loop ran, so existing `qe_pattern_embeddings` rows never populated the index and routing fell back to context-only matches. Extracted `loadEmbeddingsIntoHNSW()` and call it from both the unified and legacy paths.

- **`coverage_analyze_sublinear` and other domain MCP tools blocked by governance after 1–2 calls** — `continue-gate-integration.ts` was passing a synthetic `history.length * 500` token estimate to the guidance gate. The linear-regression slope detector saw slope = 500, threshold = 0.02, and emitted a `throttle` decision. The integration then mapped `throttle` to `shouldContinue: false`, surfacing as `Task blocked by governance: Budget acceleration detected (slope: 500.0000 > 0.02)` on legitimate first-time tool invocations. Root-cause fix: replaced the synthetic estimate with `totalTokensUsed: 0` and `budgetRemaining.tokens: MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` until real token telemetry is wired in. The coherence/uncertainty/rework checks still operate on real signals. `mapGuidanceDecision` was also corrected so `throttle` is treated as a soft slowdown hint (proceed with `throttleMs`), and only `pause`/`stop` block.

- **`test_generate_enhanced` with `framework: "jest"` produced tests that crashed at runtime** — the generator emitted `import { describe, it, expect, beforeEach } from 'jest';`, but the `'jest'` package is the CLI, not a runtime export. Tests-as-emitted failed with `Cannot find module 'jest'`. Fix: emit `from '@jest/globals'` for jest (modern jest 28+ runtime API) and `from 'vitest'` for vitest. Both the main analysis path and the stub fallback now produce framework-correct imports.

Includes 11 specialized QE agents (model-routed: 6 on Opus for heavy reasoning, 5 on Sonnet for focused execution), 9 trust-tier-2/3 skills with scoped `allowed-tools` lists, 9 `/aqe-*` slash commands, and an auto-registered MCP server entry. - **`intent-score.js` special-character corruption** — The script builder used `String.prototype.replace` with a raw substitution string, so scopes containing `$&`, `` $` ``, `$'`, or `$1-$9` corrupted the generated browser-side code. Switched to `split/join` for literal substitution.

2 isolated-vm files, parallel      6/120 =  5.0%

once -- not any single file, not the ordering, and not cumulative
isolate churn, since the serialized run does identical total work and is
clean. The rate scales with concurrent isolate count.

are serialized, leaving the other ~344 in parallel.

(p = 1.000). On the full suite, 10.0% -> 2.5% across 240 attempts
(p = 0.0088), a 75% reduction.

evidence.text: dont drop user fd until node reads a synthetic EOF (#93)
turns out https://github.com/replit/ruspty/pull/51 reduced the race rate
but did not eliminate it completely. we still see the data race bug very
rarely and it is exacerbated on high-numbers of repeats in the tests
and/or high nodejs event loop utilization
my old theory was:
- the user fd is O_NONBLOCK clear so any writes there should block until
its made its way into the 4kb intermediary buffer
- as a result, when the .wait returns, we know that the program output
has at least made it fully into the the user fd input buffer
- because we poll until `controller_inq == 0 && controller_outq == 0 &&
user_inq == 0 && user_outq == 0`, in theory we should never call the js
side exit code until theres truly nothing left in the pipe (i.e. the
readstream on the nodejs side has it in its own buffer)
HOWEVER, with some logging i saw a few cases where in fact
`controller_inq == 0 && controller_outq == 0 && user_inq == 0 &&
user_outq == 0`, the program had exited, yet the nodejs side still
missed some data
what i think is _actually_ happening is that
1. one of libuv's io threads reads the data from the controller side and
queues a data event on the stream
2. polling exits as now theres no more data in the queues we immediately
`drop(user_fd);` which [sets TTY_OTHER_CLOSED
synchronously](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/4ff71af020ae59ae2d83b174646fc2ad9fcd4dc4/drivers/tty/pty.c#L66)
and we get an error event queued on the stream
3. if the nodejs event loop happens to read error before data, we emit
'end' and mark the data as read even though technically nodejs hasnt
processed the data event yet so we drop data :(
how we fix it:
1. axe poll_pty_fds_until_read
2. make Pty struct own user_fd and expose a method for the js side to
drop this fd when its done
3. when child.wait finishes, write a synthetic 'EOF' that is actually a
custom OSC terminal control sequence (`\x1B]7878\x1B\\`, 7878 is RUST on
the phonepad :)) to the user fd (a cursory search shows no results, it
seems _very_ unlikely for this sequence to appear randomly)
4. on the nodejs wrapper side, create a transform stream that parses out
the synthetic EOF and emits it as a custom event when it happens
5. when the nodejs side hits this EOF, we know we are actually at the
end of the data stream and can safely drop user_fd
node-pty had the [same
problem](https://github.com/microsoft/node-pty/issues/72) and did the
:grug: brain thing and [added a wait
250ms](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/commit/9464b54f39d8db943ddd4c134d9bef835b7bd506
) so im calling it slightly more ok

* fix(sqlite): enable WAL + busy_timeout, apply before serving
Improves SQLite concurrency and reliability under collaborative load.
- PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL: readers no longer block writers,
dramatically reducing "database is locked" failures during concurrent
saves.
- PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000: writers wait up to 5s on contention
instead of failing immediately.
- The PRAGMAs are now awaited inside httpServer.listen() before the
server accepts requests; the previous fire-and-forget meant queries
issued in the first ~10ms of process life could still hit the default
rollback journal and timeout behaviour.
- Skip the PRAGMA on non-SQLite providers (file: URLs only) and warn on
real failures rather than silently swallowing every error — a
misconfigured database used to disappear without a trace.
Change-Id: I6ac5777aaa70ed07b85d3c062bdaf013afc169cf
Co-developed-by: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
* fix(sqlite): apply WAL/busy_timeout PRAGMAs before listen()
The previous implementation awaited configureSqlite inside the
listen() callback, which fires after the socket is already accepting
connections. Requests arriving in the small window before the PRAGMAs
finish could still hit the rollback journal and the default 0ms
busy timeout — i.e. exactly the failure mode this fix exists to
prevent.
Now configureSqlite() is awaited inside an async IIFE BEFORE listen()
runs, so the server doesn't bind the port until WAL + busy_timeout
are already in effect for the connection pool.
Change-Id: I93a3b15ddfa035ecbf4ec693d98a6c47aa7827ad
Co-developed-by: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
* build(tsc): exclude test files from production tsc
The Dockerfile production stage runs `npx tsc` to emit dist/. The same
tsc invocation was also compiling the __tests__/ tree, which made the
build fail whenever a test mock used a partial type (e.g. a Zod schema
mock with only safeParse). vitest has its own type-checking pass, so
the production build has no business compiling test files.
Exclude *.test.ts, *.integration.ts, and the __tests__/ folder. The
production tsc now succeeds even when test files have type
shortcomings; vitest still catches real test errors at run time.
Change-Id: Ica2d5f91c05131b3d9b6674df61e34fcbda60884

* fix(prisma): use $queryRawUnsafe for PRAGMA statements
Prisma's $executeRawUnsafe rejects any statement that returns a row
("Execute returned results, which is not allowed in SQLite"), and
PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL and PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000 both return
their resulting value as a row.
Production logs surfaced this as PrismaClientKnownRequestError P2010
on every startup; configureSqlite never actually applied either pragma
so the database silently kept running on the rollback journal with the
default 0ms busy timeout — i.e. exactly the failure mode this commit
chain exists to prevent.
Switch both calls to $queryRawUnsafe and discard the returned row.

Co-developed-by: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
* fix(prisma): set busy_timeout before WAL switch; use $queryRaw
Two review fixes from copilot on the bootstrap PRAGMAs:
- Order matters. PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL has to acquire the write
lock briefly. Without busy_timeout that would fail immediately on
any contention — exactly the bootstrap race the WAL change is
meant to fix. Setting busy_timeout first lets the WAL switch wait
out the initial Prisma client setup.
- Switch from $queryRawUnsafe to $queryRaw (tagged template). The
PRAGMA strings are constant so behaviour is identical, but the
tagged form rejects accidental future interpolation that would
otherwise become an SQL injection vector.
Change-Id: Ib7e25fd9ef323cd3a3e2aba249f664e2056fa539

* feat(s3): add S3 image upload support for Excalidraw drawings
Excalidraw images are stored as base64 dataURLs inside Drawing.files
(a JSON column in SQLite). One uncompressed image is several MB;
embedding many of them bloats the DB, slows collaborative sync, and
makes backups/exports unwieldy. This commit adds opt-in S3-backed
image storage. When S3_BUCKET is configured, image dataURLs go to
S3 instead of SQLite.
Architecture: backend-driven uploads. The frontend sends the entire
drawing payload (base64 dataURLs intact) to the standard create /
update / import routes; the backend uploads any new dataURLs to S3
and rewrites them to S3 URLs before persisting. Single auth boundary,
uniform coverage of paste / drag / drop / import paths, S3File rows
written by the backend in the same handler as the drawing row.
Configuration (all optional, S3 stays disabled when unset):
S3_BUCKET, S3_REGION (default us-east-1)
S3_ENDPOINT (MinIO / Cloudflare R2 / Alibaba OSS)
S3_PUBLIC_URL (CDN base; unset → private-bucket redirect mode)
S3_FORCE_PATH_STYLE (MinIO needs true; OSS needs false)
S3_KEY_PREFIX (default "excalidash")
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
Backend module (backend/src/s3.ts):
- Typed S3Config, presigned URL helpers, uploadBuffer / listS3Objects
utilities, shared FILE_KEY_PREFIX / buildS3Key / drawingS3Prefix so
upload and cleanup paths can't drift onto different prefixes.
Backend integration:
- backend/src/fileProcessing.ts: processFilesForS3(files, userId,
drawingId, prisma) scans the file record for base64 dataURLs,
uploads them, upserts a row keyed (drawingId, fileId) in S3File,
returns a rewritten file record (base64 → S3 URL).
- Wired into POST /drawings, PUT /drawings/:id, and both /import/*
routes so every code path that introduces a new image is covered.
New routes (backend/src/routes/files.ts):
- GET /files/config: surfaces s3Enabled for frontend feature
detection.
- GET /files/:fileId: 302 redirects to a presigned GET URL for
private-bucket deployments where the dataURL stored on the drawing
is /api/files/:fileId.
Schema (backend/prisma/schema.prisma + initial migration):
- New S3File table mapping fileId → s3Key + userId + mimeType so the
redirect route can resolve the bucket location. Additive only; no
destructive changes to existing tables.
Sanitiser (backend/src/security.ts):
- Permits the new "https://..." (CDN) and "/api/files/..."
(redirect) shapes as safe dataURL values without otherwise
loosening the existing image-dataURL validation.
Object key layout: {prefix}/{userId}/{drawingId}/{fileId}.{ext},
served with Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable since
fileIds are content hashes and the objects are never mutated in
place.
When S3 is enabled there is no silent base64 fallback: upload
failures surface to the user instead of pretending the image was
persisted.
Change-Id: I189e27b1f5459a1782e4a69d1f8c4494dee3921e

* fix(s3): validate fileId before using as S3 key segment
Reject file ids that don't match /^[\w-]{1,200}$/ in two layers, so a
request body like
files: { "../../etc/passwd": { dataURL: "data:image/png;base64,..." } }
cannot escape the per-user S3 prefix and write outside it:
- security.ts sanitizeDrawingData drops malformed keys before
persistence, so the drawing.files JSON cannot store entries that
would later be uploaded under attacker-controlled paths.
- fileProcessing.processFilesForS3 also drops them defensively, since

Same regex used by the GET /files/:fileId route param. Adds a

* fix(files): authorise GET /files/:fileId via drawing access, not by guessability
Excalidraw fileIds are SHA-1 hashes of the file bytes — anyone in
possession of the original image can compute the id, so the previous
"fileId is unguessable" comment was incorrect and any authenticated
user could fetch images uploaded by anyone else.
Now the route authorises by drawing access:
- the uploader (S3File.userId === req.user.id) can always read; OR
- the caller has access to a drawing that references this fileId, either
one they own or one explicitly shared with them via DrawingPermission.
A single substring query on the JSON columns is enough because fileIds
are >= 16 random chars; the wrapping quotes prevent prefix collisions
(`abc1` won't match `abc12`).
Also adds a 401 fallback in case requireAuth is ever removed.

* fix(files): allow link-share viewers to fetch private-bucket images
GET /files/:fileId previously required a logged-in user via requireAuth,
which broke private-bucket deployments whenever a drawing was shared
with an active link-share: the anonymous viewer could open the
drawing scene but every returned 401.
Replace requireAuth with optionalAuth and decide access by drawing
membership instead:
- The uploader (S3File.userId === caller) always has access.
- Authenticated callers also pass if they own a drawing referencing
the fileId, or were granted access via DrawingPermission.
- Anyone (anonymous included) passes if a drawing referencing the
fileId has an active DrawingLinkShare row (revokedAt IS NULL and
expiresAt either NULL or in the future).
- Otherwise return 404 so the response doesn't leak whether a fileId
exists for someone who doesn't have access.

* fix(import): pre-resolve drawing id, bound parallel S3 uploads
Two import flows (excalidash backup + legacy SQLite) both pre-uploaded
files to S3 using the imported drawing id, then on a foreign-owner id
collision wrote the row under a fresh uuidv4() — leaving every uploaded
object as a permanent S3 orphan keyed under an id that no DB row knew
about.
Now both routes pre-resolve the final drawing id before uploading by
peeking at any pre-existing drawing of the same id; if it belongs to
another user, we generate the UUID up front and feed it to both the
upload and the in-transaction create. The transaction still re-checks
authoritatively, but always writes under the same finalId.

batches of 8. A 5000-drawing import previously serialised every S3 PUT
inside the request, easily hitting reverse-proxy timeouts; the bound
keeps memory and socket pressure flat without saturating the bucket.

* fix(drawings): copy S3 storage on duplicate so the original can be deleted
POST /drawings/:id/duplicate previously copied elements/appState/files
verbatim, including the dataURLs that point at the *original*
drawing's S3 prefix (`/api/files/origId/fileId` or
`https://.../excalidash/owner/origId/fileId.ext`). The duplicate's
images therefore pointed at storage owned by the original. Deleting
the original then ran the new prefix-scoped S3 cleanup and silently
broke every image in the duplicate.

S3File row of the original under the new drawingId path, writes a
fresh (newDrawingId, fileId) S3File row, and rewrites the dataURLs
in the new drawing's files JSON to match the new drawing id. Each
drawing — original and duplicate — owns its own storage from the
moment of duplication, so DELETE /drawings/:origId can no longer
strand the duplicate.

CopyObject; no download/re-upload).

* fix(drawings): rewrite preview SVG so it doesn't inline base64 after S3 upload
Symptom: every save produced a megabyte-scale `Drawing.preview`
column. The SVG had `<image href="data:image/png;base64,...">` for
each image element instead of the S3 URL.
Root cause: the frontend generates the preview SVG from the canvas
state at save time, before the round-trip uploads files to S3. The
SVG embeds whatever dataURL the file currently has, which at save
time is still base64. processFilesForS3 only rewrites the dataURL
inside `Drawing.files`, never the parallel preview SVG, so the
inlined base64 stays in the preview forever.
Add a rewritePreviewForS3 helper in fileProcessing.ts that diffs the
original-vs-processed files map and applies the resulting URL
substitutions to the preview string. Wire it into the POST and PUT
handlers so the preview saved alongside the upload reflects the same
S3 URLs as Drawing.files.
Best-effort string substitution: it works because the same dataURL
string is character-identical in both `files[fileId].dataURL` and the
preview SVG's href. If frontend encoding ever diverges, the worst
case is the preview is left as-is — never crashes.

* fix(drawings): roll back duplicate when an S3 copy fails
The duplicate handler used to "log and continue" when copyS3Object
threw — the duplicated `Drawing.files` JSON kept the original
drawing's dataURL for that fileId, the new drawing landed pointing at
the original's S3 prefix, and the next deletion of the original
silently broke the duplicate's images.
Restructure the flow so the new drawing row is only created after
every S3 copy succeeds:
1. Pre-allocate the new drawing id with crypto.randomUUID().
2. Copy every S3 object to the new prefix; track the destination
keys in a list as we go.
3. If any copy throws, delete every key we managed to copy so the
bucket isn't left with orphan objects, and return 500. The
original drawing is never touched.
4. Only after all copies succeed, open a single Prisma transaction
that creates the drawing row and the S3File rows together — so a
DB failure can't leave S3 objects with no row, and the new
drawing is always observable in a fully-consistent state.

* fix(import): regenerate drawing id inside the transaction on race conflict
The earlier fix pre-resolved a final drawing id before uploading to
S3 so the upload key and the eventual DB row would match. That works
for the common case, but if a drawing with the same id is created
between the pre-check and the in-transaction findUnique (race), the
in-tx tx.drawing.create({ id: finalId }) hits a unique-constraint
error and aborts the whole import — so a stray race kills the whole
batch.
In the conflict branch (existing.userId !== req.user.id), check
whether the pre-resolved finalId still equals the imported id: if so,
the pre-upload check missed the race and we'd be writing under a
guaranteed conflict. Generate a fresh UUID for the row instead. The
S3 objects we already PUT under the imported-id path become orphans
that the storage-management tools can sweep up; that's vastly better
than failing the whole batch.
Applied to both /import/excalidash and /import/sqlite/legacy.

* fix(s3): preserve S3File rows during composite-PK migration
The previous shape of 20260506130000_s3file_composite_pk did
DROP TABLE + CREATE TABLE, which silently lost every existing
(fileId → s3Key, mimeType, userId) mapping. For private-bucket
deployments that turns every /api/files/:drawingId/:fileId into a
404 until each affected drawing is re-saved.
Replace the drop with a copy: extract the drawingId from each
s3Key (which has shape `{prefix}/{userId}/{drawingId}/{fileId}.{ext}`)
by chaining INSTR + SUBSTR three times — SQLite has no native
split() and the bundled engine doesn't have REVERSE either, so we
walk the string from the start. Rows whose s3Key doesn't have at
least three '/' are skipped (they can only come from a custom
S3_KEY_PREFIX containing '/', which would otherwise misattribute the
drawingId; operators in that case still need to re-save).
INSERT OR IGNORE protects against duplicate (drawingId, fileId)
pairs theoretically allowed under the old schema; the survivor wins.

chdb/durable/node: the engine a Node caller should not have to write
The control plane takes an injected `EngineAdapter` and that stays true — but
"injected" does not have to mean "hand-written". `chdb/durable/node` is the
adapter over this package's own addon, so a Node caller supplies a factory
instead of a symbol table:
new DurableNamespace(url, { engineFactory: nodeEngineFactory() })
It sits behind its own subpath rather than in the barrel because importing it
*does* load the addon, and putting it in `chdb/durable` would make that
subpath's no-native-load guarantee vacuous. `test/durable/subpath.test.ts`
still asserts that guarantee in a child process with `process.dlopen`
replaced by a throw.
Two things the adapter owns rather than the ABI. First, connect-time
settings: `--backups.allowed_path`, plus the four that mean "the statement
landed before it returned" — without them a statement could reach the WAL
while its local effect is not yet in the database the next checkpoint
archives. Second, the quoting for the two statements with no C entry point,
`CREATE DATABASE` and `USE`. That quoting has to agree with the quoting core
does for BACKUP and RESTORE, and a backslash is where it can silently
disagree: doubling backticks alone leaves `\d` an escape sequence, so a
database named `od\d-db` would be created under a name the backup call would
not find. Both escapes, and the suite round-trips a name carrying both.
`close()` waits out any call still on a libuv thread rather than releasing
the handle under it. There is no interrupt for a running query, so waiting is
the only correct answer; the alternative is a use-after-free.
An addon predating this ABI is refused by name, with both remedies, because
the loader prefers a published `@chdb/lib-*` prebuilt over a local build —
so that refusal is the first thing a developer in a checkout meets, and
"undefined is not a function" would not help.
The new suite runs the load-bearing scenarios over the addon rather than
every scenario twice; the Bun suite already proves the state machine against
real core through a different seam. `npm run test:durable:node`, its own
vitest project because it is the one durable suite that loads native code and
the engine binds one data path per process. CI runs it on two platforms, and
the engine release check runs it too — four C entry points and a
size-versioned struct are exactly what a new core can break without breaking
any declaration the addon compiles against.

evidence.text: ci(pytest): speed up the back-end test jobs DEV-3144 (#7724)
### 💭 Notes
**Matrix rebalance.** The 5 `test-path` groups are now split by measured
run time instead of by directory. Their local times were between roughly
330s and 720s, and they are now between roughly 330s and 465s:
- `kpi/tests/api/` without `test_api_exports.py`
- `kpi/tests/` without `kpi/tests/api/`
- `kobo/apps/openrosa/`
- `kobo/apps/subsequences/`, `kobo/apps/organizations/`,
`kobo/apps/trash_bin/`
- `hub/`, the rest of `kobo/apps/`, and
`kpi/tests/api/v2/test_api_exports.py`
`kpi/tests/api/test_api_current_user.py` was never run in CI, because
the old third group used `--ignore=kpi/tests/api/`. It now runs in the
first group. `test_api_exports.py` sits in the last group because
`--ignore` also skips paths passed explicitly, so it cannot be added
back to a group that ignores one of its parent directories. With
`--collect-only`, the union of the 5 groups matches the full suite (3711
tests), with no duplicates and nothing missing.
**Template test DB.** The root `conftest.py` overrides
`django_db_setup`. Under xdist, pytest-django migrates one test database
per worker, which takes about a minute each. Instead, the first worker
that takes an `fcntl` lock migrates a template database (`<test
db>_template`) and creates the `user_reports` materialized view in it.
No test runs on it. Every worker then gets its own test database as a
copy of it, with `CREATE DATABASE ... WITH TEMPLATE`, which takes
seconds. The other workers wait on the lock during the build, because
Postgres refuses to copy a database that another session is connected
to, and the copies then run one after the other. The xdist controller
drops the template database in `pytest_sessionfinish`. Without xdist
(including the `--lf` rerun step), or when it reuses existing databases
(`--reuse-db` without `--create-db`), the fixture behaves like
pytest-django's default. Teardown follows pytest-django too: with
`--reuse-db`, the databases are kept, even when `--create-db` rebuilt
them. No test uses `serialized_rollback`, so the template database is
created without Django's DB serialization.
**Coverage on `main` only.** `pytest.yml` gets a `coverage` input, off
by default, and only `ci-main.yml` turns it on. PR runs, and
`release-2-stabilize.yml`, no longer pass `--cov` or upload to
Coveralls. Branch coverage (`branch = True` in `.coveragerc`) made two
groups about 40% slower locally, and Coveralls posts no status or
comment on PRs, so PR coverage never showed up in reviews. `main` still
gets one Coveralls build per commit. On CI, without coverage, the 10
pytest steps were 20% faster the three previous runs (and the slowest
was ~30% faster).
**Distribution mode.** `--dist=loadfile` is kept: it is the fastest and
most predictable mode for this suite, while `load` splits test classes
across workers and repeats their class-level setup, and `loadscope`
caused parallelization problems.
**Splitting large test files was tried and dropped.** Under `loadfile` a
test file is atomic, so splitting `test_api_submissions.py` into three
files made the first group about 60 to 80s faster on CI. The slowest job
did not change, though: with balanced groups, runner noise (about 15%
between two runs of the same commit) decides which job finishes last.
The split was reverted to keep this PR small and avoid conflicts with
other open PRs that touch that file.
Claude Opus 5.5 contributed to these changes, but @noliveleger takes
full responsibility for them.

evidence.text: - name: Test progress publication through Marina and Postgres
[rl] Run Snowball experiments from presets and publish results (#10740)
To compare changes to Snowball’s inference engine, trainer or training
data, run experiments from named presets with recorded inputs and saved
results.
`rl.py` holds no model settings: each model file (here `snowball_rl.py`)
declares its presets, controls and model name, and calls the shared
runner, which handles planning, submission, waiting and status. The
model name labels the W&B run, the finelog records, the Marina row and
each evaluation row, so two models' runs stay separate in every sink.
Snowball's presets form two groups. The short loop (also called the
quick loop) compares one change against control runs: generation speed,
training speed, learning and data screening. The long loop trains a
model and keeps its best checkpoint: `train-long` evaluates the 100-task
EvalLite active set at step 0 and every ten updates, records the best
eligible step and exports that step to Hugging Face format. Every
Snowball preset restricts NCCL to the InfiniBand rails
(`NCCL_IB_HCA=ibp`).
`--plan` composes each launch on CPU and runs the training driver's own
configuration checks, so a setting the driver would refuse, such as a
batch smaller than the data-parallel size or an unknown Harbor task
setting, fails before any GPU is requested. Before a gated submission,
the launcher composes the candidate on CPU and checks that the saved
control runs named by the preset's control pin match the current preset
configuration. After the runs finish, the comparison requires matching
evaluation requests and held-out task content, then saves the
measurements and a verdict with its reasons. The checked-in pins are for
`2026.11.06.1`. Until pins for the current preset revision,
`2026.11.20.3`, are checked in, gated launches and control publication
stop and print the command that collects them.
At the end of `--run --wait`, the launcher publishes available terminal
attempts for `learning-medium`, `data-medium` and `train-long` using the
caller's Marina login. The `publish` command also sends a selected
stored attempt or the pinned learning controls. Marina groups records by
run and lets readers pick an attempt to see its evaluation scores,
available verdict and failed checks. Records can link to the W&B run,
Grafana window, experiment issue and EvalDash runs. A GitHub experiment
issue is optional: `--issue N` links the run to it, and the run-rl skill
asks the experimenter whether to open a new issue, use an existing one
or not track the run, then posts one comment per result with a fixed set
of fields after the experimenter approves it.
The `compare` command recomputes a candidate's verdict from saved
outputs on CPU. The EvalLite scorer reports coverage for a chosen
version and computes its score when every active task has verified
answers with the matching task ID and content digest. [RL experiment
recipe](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/82a60d0c42c2d04aee8e2913ef1cd1792c291a81/docs/recipes/rl-experiments.md)

runner-pod plan.

all 14 request-path benchmarks to it. Also loop the sub-100µs
serialization and routing-trie benchmarks internally so each measured

fix(plugin): forward the xdist plugin when gremlin runs inherit -p no:xdist (#928)
## Summary
When ini `addopts` or `PYTEST_ADDOPTS` holds `-p no:xdist` and the
session loads xdist anyway (`-p xdist` on the command line), gremlin
runs inherited the block, so `-n` from the session failed with
"unrecognized arguments" or tests that use xdist fixtures errored.
Gremlin runs now get the xdist loader and `-n 0` in that case.
- The block is read the way pytest reads `-p`: the last value naming
`xdist` or `xdist.plugin` decides, in both the spaced and attached
spellings. A later `-p xdist` lifts an earlier `-p no:xdist`.
- `-p no:xdist.plugin` does not count as a block, because it does not
hide xdist under autoload.
- Only affected sessions get the existing `xdist-668` cache key part.
Every other session keeps a byte-identical key.
- The scenario in the issue (autoload off, `-n` on the command line) was
already fixed by #925; its regression test is kept.
- `PYTEST_PLUGINS=xdist` did not reproduce; regression tests only.
## Changes
- `src/pytest_gremlins/plugin.py`:
`_gremlin_runs_inherit_an_xdist_block`, and `_xdist_options_for`
forwards the loader when gremlin runs inherit a block.
- `tests/plugin/test_xdist_autoload.py`,
`tests/plugin/test_xdist_inherited_autoload.py` (new): unit and
end-to-end tests.
- `tests/cache/test_cache_version_guard.py`: re-recorded `plugin.py`
digest. No `CACHE_VERSION` or `RUNNER_FIDELITY_VERSION` change. The next
release needs a `(cache kept: ...)` line: only sessions that inherit an
xdist block get the new key part.
- Docs: `docs/api/cache.md`, `docs/guide/troubleshooting.md`.
## Type of Change
- [x] Bug fix

everything after them, installed once the population is complete; the
persistence toggle, which changes the build's own saves, once the build
has finished;

of the sequence to it, and each build resets the IDs it skips;
- relationship-search updates (IndexRelationship, RemoveRelationship,
storage events included) are ordered in the same sequence;

* storage: one read snapshot of the committed and write-behind state
ReadSnapshotter opens a ReadSnapshotView over the storage capture owner:
a long-lived read view (captureReadView with longLived) and the whole
write-behind overlay, selected at the same point under the buffer's lock.
Nodes and edges are read through it (IterateNodes, StreamEdges) for as
long as it is open. Between scans the view holds only its registered read
timestamp, which keeps compaction from discarding a version it can see
until Close; each scan opens its own transaction at it, so engine Close
waits for a scan in progress, never for the snapshot's lifetime.
BadgerEngine implements it; WALEngine, NamespacedEngine (scoped to its
namespace), MemoryEngine, TracedEngine, ReplicatedEngine and the
multidb size-tracking engine forward it, with compile-time assertions.
CompositeEngine and RemoteEngine do not: OpenReadSnapshot reports
ErrReadSnapshotUnsupported for them.

* search: the build reads one storage snapshot and applies queued writes after it
The build read its nodes and its stored relationships in separate reads,
drained queued writes between node batches and skipped stored copies the
queue had overtaken. Its baseline could combine a node and a
relationship that never coexisted in storage, and the skip sets and the
eager relationship copy held memory outside the queue's bound.
Now the queue opens, then the build opens one storage read snapshot
(storage.ReadSnapshotter) and installs its baseline from it: the nodes,
then the stored relationships, streamed. A write whose search call ran
before the queue opened committed before the snapshot, which holds it;
every write queued after is applied once, after the baseline, in arrival
order. There are no drains between batches and no skip sets.
On an engine without read snapshots (CompositeEngine, RemoteEngine) the
build has no point to order queued writes against: writes made during
it wait for it, as before writes were queued.
The queue reserves, when it opens, what the runtime soft memory limit
leaves above the live heap. Every retained copy counts against it,
relationship-search updates included (orderRelationshipUpdate); a copy
past it waits for the build. With no limit configured the queue is not
bounded beyond the process's memory.
SetIndexFlags decides the change it reports in the section that queues
its flags, so concurrent calls each report their own transition.
The sequence guard proves that an entry call dominates each index write
(an if or switch branch the call does not dominate, code before it,
closures started before it and any goto are reported).

no growth. It now overwrites an 8,000-node store of 8 KiB incompressible

* search: the queue counts the heap its copies hold
The reservation bounds what the queue retains only if the bytes it counts
for a copy cover what the copy holds. They did not: a copied map's slot
storage (groups of eight slots, filled to seven of eight) was counted as
a key header per entry, and the entry and struct copy as a fixed 256
bytes. A queued relationship-search update with a 1024-dimension vector
held 4,639 bytes and was counted as 4,393, so a full reservation
overshot by about 5%.
Copied maps now count their header and slot groups (queuedMapBytes), the
entry counts twice its size for the slice's spare capacity, and a node or
edge copy counts its struct (unsafe.Sizeof). Chunk embeddings count their
slice headers, labels theirs.
TestBuildQueuedCopiesCountTheirHeap (TestPopulationOrderQueuedCopiesCountTheirHeap
on develop) measures 4,000 queued copies of each kind: counted 4,729 B
against 4,704 B held per relationship update, 2,421 B against 2,358 B
per node write.

search.Service.RefreshNode/RefreshEdge reserve a per-ID generation, read
storage, then index or remove through #1475's readLockOrQueue as ordinary
writes. A queued write carries valid (claim): the build installs it only while
its reservation is the newest and skips a superseded one. The
relationship-search part is ordered the same way (current). A refresh whose
reservation a newer, applied refresh retired reads nothing; one whose read
fails is retried by the database's search owner, not lost.

and relationship suppression in both directions, decay flips, sidecar writes
and a namespace reset on DeleteByPrefix, which returns once the reset was
consumed. The DB subscribes through storage.EventSubscriber, which every
engine wrapper forwards (ReplicatedEngine and the multidb size tracker
included; Open fails if one does not), so HA primaries and standbys deliver
events too. Cypher refreshes after commit, including kp.suppress(r); orphan
cleanup, DB admin, retention and every Qdrant point writer refresh.

its persisted files (one directory per generation, named by CURRENT), pending
and retried refreshes, and a generation. A reset, a restore (once storage
is replaced) and a prefix delete end it through one invalidate step,
which also covers databases whose state is only persisted. Executors resolve
the service on each use (SetSearchServiceResolver), so none keeps a replaced
one, and the Cypher result cache keys by service instance.
Guards, each mutation-tested: storage mutator population (type-resolved, with
a scenario or a reasoned exclusion per member), wrapper forwarding (AST over
pkg/ and cmd/), no consumer keeping a *search.Service, the DB consumption
matrix (standalone, in-memory, HA primary, HA standby), cold and warm reset
and restore, retries, payload callers and Qdrant point writers.

their maps when no producer has already created the next batch; newer queued
reservations and retries retain their own maps. Empty maps retain capacity

* fix(fabric): preserve composite CALL rows, OPTIONAL CALL, UNION semantics and participant completion (v1.4.4) (#1484)
fix(fabric): preserve composite CALL rows, OPTIONAL CALL, UNION semantics and participant completion
A composite CALL's outer continuation runs over the complete input stream,
so WITH ... ORDER BY followed by an aggregating RETURN aggregates once
(#1479). A CALL body that is a UNION is split into branches, each planned on
its own USE target (#1480). Fabric reads a name spelled UNION, OPTIONAL or
RETURN with the Cypher executor's canonical keyword-name reader, so
parameters, variables and keys named union stay names.
Every Fabric UNION route ends in one merge with the single-graph UNION
contract the Cypher executor supplies: columns match by name, other names
are DifferentColumnsInUnion, and DISTINCT compares rows by equivalence. A
level that mixes UNION and UNION ALL is rejected with the single-graph
InvalidClauseComposition error before any branch is planned or runs.
A unit CALL runs its body for the body's effects and keeps each input row
exactly once, whatever rows the body produces internally; its columns are
its input's. OPTIONAL CALL keeps an input row whose returning body has no
rows, with null for the body's columns. The APPLY batching rewrites skip
both.
Remote participants complete with their transaction: like local
participants, they keep the enlisting context's values but not its
cancellation, bounded by the remote request timeout, so an APPLY batch or a
finished HTTP request can no longer cancel COMMIT or ROLLBACK. Shared
explicit-transaction and remote dispatch is serialized, and the branch trace
flag is atomic.

* fix(cypher): concurrent MERGE writers of one node wait instead of failing with UNIQUE (v1.4.4) (#1673)
* fix(cypher): serialize concurrent MERGE writers of one node instead of failing (NOR-117)
Concurrent identical MERGE statements on a uniquely constrained key failed
at commit with a UNIQUE violation when the statement also wrote the node it
matched (ON MATCH SET, or a later SET/REMOVE/DELETE of it). A MERGE that
found the node committed matched it without the key's lock, so two such
statements wrote the node from the same snapshot and the later commit lost
the write-write race, reported as "claimed by concurrent commit". Neo4j
5.26 makes the later statement wait, and both succeed.
prepareMergeKeys, the shared MERGE key owner of the node, path and pattern
routes, now takes the key's lock even when the node exists when the
statement writes it (storage PrepareMergeNodeForWrite): the next writer
waits, catches up to the previous commit and writes on top of it.
mergeNodeWritesOf reads once per statement which MERGE variables it
writes; MERGEs that only read their node keep the lock-free match.
A test-only hook (storage.SetUniqueKeyLockWaitHookForTesting) lets tests
order concurrent statements by the key wait instead of timing. Regression
tests cover Execute, Bolt and HTTP, auto-commit and explicit transactions.

* fix(fabric): preserve remote CALL scope and value types in v1.4.4 (#1630)
* fix(fabric): bind remote CALL imports and keep outer variables after CALL
A CALL body that runs on a remote constituent imports outer variables, but
the remote statement received the row's values only as parameters named
like the variables, so it rejected them as undefined, and the row values
replaced the caller's parameters of the same name.
Imports come from the Cypher executor's CALL subquery reader, the one its
single-database CALL execution uses, installed on the Fabric planner: the
scope clause of CALL (x) / (*) / () or the body's importing WITH (WITH x,
WITH *), read with comments as whitespace, so the result is the same with
query normalization on or off. A scope clause's variables stay visible
throughout the body: every fragment of a scoped body runs on the remote as
WITH $p AS x CALL (x) { ... } RETURN *, and the imported columns are left
out of its result. The importing-WITH form projects its imports ahead of
the body.
Every name Fabric adds to a statement (import parameters, the APPLY
pipeline's key, rows and row-wrapper names) is one that occurs nowhere in
the statement and is not a caller parameter or row variable, and no user
variable is filtered by a reserved-looking prefix. The APPLY pipeline's
row wrapper is marked on its result (ResultStream.RowWrapper) and carried
through APPLY inputs and UNION branches, never recognized by column name.
Values reach a remote participant as statement parameters, the caller's
and the imported row's alike, and the remote transport is the one owner
of how each travels (storage.RemoteParameterValue). Bolt and HTTP values
typed by the row metadata reach Fabric as one storage.RemoteTypedValue,
which the Cypher executor decodes into its temporal and point values, at
any nesting depth. A node, relationship or path is rejected with Neo4j's
invalid-import error (Neo.ClientError.Statement.TypeError, GQL status
Neo4j's HTTP API tells an integer from a float by the number's form. The
HTTP transport reads JSON numbers losslessly, in rows, nested values and
graph entities: an integer is an exact int64 and a number with a fraction
or an exponent a float64. It writes float parameters as JSON floats, so
an integral float stays a float, and a nil list or map parameter of any
type is still written as null, so SET n.p = $x removes the property. A
value relayed through an HTTP participant keeps its type and all 64 bits.
Batched correlated lookups key numbers by Cypher equality, through the
numeric equivalence keys the Cypher executor's value keys use (moved to
9007199254740992.0 do not, and NaN matches nothing, whichever transport
returned the value.
The planner recognizes CALL (x) { }, CALL (*) { } and CALL () { } with
their scope clause, so a scoped body with its own USE is planned like any
other CALL body instead of re-entering the composite in an explicit
transaction.
The rows a composite statement's leading part hands to a CALL kept only
the aliases of its last WITH, even when another clause followed it:
USE comp WITH 'ab' AS s UNWIND [1,2] AS x CALL { ... } RETURN s lost s.
A WITH now gives the leading part's columns only when it is its last
clause, its WHERE, ORDER BY, SKIP and LIMIT aside; otherwise every
variable in scope is kept.
Every temporal, spatial and duration value, a pointer to one included,
reaches a participant as its Cypher type in any parameter position, also
inside lists and maps. The Bolt transport sends each as the Neo4j Go
driver does (time.Time, dbtype.Date, ...), copying a parameter map only
when a value changes, and sends a nil pointer, list or map as null. Neo4j's
HTTP API reads parameters as plain JSON, so the HTTP transport sends such a
value, or a NaN or infinite float, as the JSON its constructor reads, and
writes each reference to that parameter as the constructor over it: an
atom valid wherever a parameter is (a map literal in CREATE (n $props), a
list comprehension for a batch of rows), whose text depends on the
values' types, not on how many rows a batch has. Time and datetime
offsets keep their seconds (+02:05:59, a historical zone's local mean
time).
A CALL scope clause item that is not a variable (CALL (1), CALL (x + 1),
CALL (x, *)), or an empty one (CALL (x,), CALL (,x), CALL (x,,y)), is
Neo4j's syntax error, reported by the scope clause reader that statement
validation, single-database execution and Fabric planning all read scope
clauses with. A scope variable the query doesn't define is Neo4j's
compile-time "Variable `x` not defined", reported where statements are
checked: a composite statement is checked as the one statement it is
without its USE clauses (FabricPlanner.SingleGraphStatement) before it
plans, enlists a participant or runs any part, and EXPLAIN and PROFILE
check the statement they plan, so the error comes before a missing
parameter and before any write. A word such as null, true, NaN or
Infinity is a variable's name there, as in Neo4j: unquoted, it imports
the variable the query binds quoted (WITH 1 AS `NaN` CALL (NaN) { ... }).

* fix(storage,cypher): hidden-ID creates keep the stored entity
A CREATE over the ID of a stored hidden node returns ErrAlreadyExists, as
before hidden records were readable.
A CREATE over the ID of a stored hidden relationship is an idempotent no-op
when the image the transaction would commit (type, endpoints and properties;
timestamps and visibility bookkeeping excluded) equals the stored body. A
different image fails permanently with HiddenEdgeIdentityConflictError
(Neo.ClientError.Schema.ConstraintValidationFailed), so MERGE does not retry
it. The relationship stays hidden and nothing is published: no body, index,
count, callback or WAL entry.
BadgerTransaction owns the decision. The candidate is kept in a hidden-only
slot, never in pendingEdges or another visible read overlay; SET through the
MERGE's own binding updates it, DELETE drops it, and commit compares the
final image with the latest stored predecessor, both as the property codec
stores them, so the same list, number or temporal value never differs only in
its Go representation. Transactions whose only work is such a candidate
still reach commit validation. Cypher MERGE reports no
CREATE/SET stats for the no-op and never caches the candidate as a match, so
repeated rows and statements re-enter the same disposition, ON MATCH never
fires and a later MATCH does not see it.
Every acknowledged body is published as the image storage returns for it,
by one owner (writtenNodeImage, writtenEdgeImage) at every ingress: the
transaction commit, synchronous or write-behind (before MVCC history,
change events, the overlay, caches and callbacks), direct and bulk engine
writes (from their final bytes, a suppression rescore included), follower
apply and WAL replay through those paths, and recovery. A body of scalar
values (strings, booleans, null, numbers of any width) that carries no
embedding state is the writer's own body, which the write path already
owns, given those values: its integers as stored reads return them (a
property map it holds is replaced, never modified) and its timestamps in
the codec's zone and precision; any other is decoded from the bytes the
write already encoded, keeping the writer's runtime embedding identity,
which is never encoded. The entity caches store what they are given, so
the separate list normalisation they applied is gone: a cached read now
returns what an uncached read decodes. Stored reads, quota accounting and
the identity check therefore see the same body however it is served; quota
sizes a prior as read and images only what it stages.
Behaviour change (Go API): a value written through the Go storage API reads
back right after the write as storage returns it, as it did after a cache
eviction or restart (a generic string list as []string, a custom zone
without its name), Bolt and HTTP results unchanged. Every stored integer
reads as int64, as Cypher integers are, whatever code msgpack wrote it in;
only a value above MaxInt64 reads as uint64. A float32 list reads as
[]float32, as float64, integer, string and bool lists keep their type (an
imported vector came back as []interface{}). The decoder applies this, so
older data reads the same way and the write encoding is unchanged. Integer
widths had broken type switches after any restart (a Qdrant collection's
dimensions, payload lists, numeric fast paths), and a decoded temporal's
own zone never matched as a property index key: indexes now key temporals
by kind, instant, offset and text, and numeric conversions accept every
width.
Every read that merges the write-behind overlay applies the visibility of
its storage path through one composition (overlay_visibility.go): MERGE
identity reads (GetEdgesBetween, GetEdgeBetween, MatchEdgesBetween), point
reads, scans, streams, adjacency and snapshots. A guard test fails on any
other reader of the buffer's bodies.
Every create reads storage for its ID, a UUID-shaped stable or imported ID
included, except one the executor minted for it: CREATE and MERGE pass the
IDs they generate through the transaction's CreateMinted* operations,
which keep the pending, batch and endpoint checks and skip only the stored
read. storage.Engine offers no minted create, so replication, WAL replay,
imports and remote writes always read.
The candidate check costs ordinary writes nothing: the candidate map is
allocated only when a candidate is staged, and the namespaced engine keeps
its ID prefix instead of building it on every prefix check and count read.
The conflict message is in the en-US, es-ES and en-XA catalogs.
Buffered WAL records that carry replaces_existing are still decoded for count
replay; no writer emits the flag.

* fix(storage): order every write after acknowledged write-behind commits
With write-behind enabled, a write that commits to Badger itself lost to the
replay of an older acknowledged commit of the same entity: a direct
CreateNode/UpdateNode/DeleteNode/CreateEdge/UpdateEdge/DeleteEdge, an explicit
transaction commit, an implicit commit the buffer does not take, or the decay
suppression rewrite. A direct or explicit delete succeeded and released
quota, but the older buffered update still served reads, rejected a
re-create of the ID as occupied, and wrote the deleted record back when it
flushed; a later update was overwritten the same way, and a deleted node
kept the relationships a buffered commit gave it.
The write-behind buffer now owns that order through per-entity stripes
(orderAfterBufferedCommits). A commit the buffer acknowledges holds the
stripes of its entities shared; a write that commits to Badger itself holds
the stripes of the entities it touches (relationship endpoints and a deleted
node's relationships included) exclusively until it has committed and
reserved its notifications, and first drains the buffer when a generation
not yet applied holds one of them. Writes of different entities never wait
for each other. A transaction that drained moves its commit onto Badger
transactions opened afterwards and checks its snapshot conflicts again
against the drained heads. Every writer takes the locks in one order (write
barrier, unique-constraint locks, order stripes, commit gate); the replay
takes no stripe. Without write-behind nothing is taken.
A write that replaces or removes stored state wholesale (DeleteByPrefix,
Restore, RebuildMVCCHeads) is a lifecycle write (beginLifecycleWrite): it
holds the write barrier exclusively and every stripe, and applies every
acknowledged commit first. A transaction open across a prefix delete of its
namespace fails its commit with a conflict instead of committing records
encoded with the dropped dictionaries. Backup applies the acknowledged
commits first, so every write acknowledged before it is in it. Close stops
admitting writes before its final drain, so a listener that writes from that
drain is rejected rather than acknowledged into a generation nothing drains.
The low-level MVCC writers (append version/tombstone, update current head)
take the entity order; WriteMVCCHead, which the lifecycle pruner calls with
a head it read earlier, takes it too and never moves a head backwards.
Commits validate their final image when they are acknowledged or committed:
every relationship they leave has both endpoints, and a node they delete has
no relationship outside its cascade. A body the transaction superseded, or a
relationship it moved away from the node it deletes, is not checked. A
commit that writes an entity a commit acknowledged after it began deleted,
while the buffer still holds that delete, fails with a conflict: committing
over it would bring the entity back without counting it, or delete and count
it twice. A transaction's update of a node it deleted changes nothing, as
in Neo4j (#907): it brought the node back without counting it. An
acknowledged re-create of a deleted node is a relationship endpoint before
it is applied.
A buffered relationship update now shadows its stored adjacency at the
endpoints it left, and adjacency reads list a relationship at a node only
while its body has the node at that end, so a node delete no longer cascades
to a relationship an acknowledged commit moved away (the move was lost on
flush), and a stale adjacency cache entry at the old endpoint no longer
fails a valid delete.
Listeners run at one publication point outside every ordering lock: a write
holds a place in the notification order from its write barrier until it
released every lock, and completing it delivers its own events and those of
the commits its drain applied; a replay only queues its events. A listener
may therefore write back to the entity it is told about without deadlocking
the engine. Tests install a tracker that fails when any listener runs on a
goroutine holding a write-order stripe or the commit gate.
A deleted entity's on-demand suppression no longer ends in a detached
goroutine per delete, which could delete the suppression an entity created
again with the same ID was given afterwards, and was lost when the store
closed first: one worker deletes the ended keys, ordered with every
suppression write and lifecycle write, and Close runs it. A prefix delete
ends the suppression of the entities it deletes; before, an entity created
again under the prefix was hidden. Restore folds the derived-count deltas
it loads, as open does: a new delta reused a restored delta's key and the
counters underflowed at the next open.
A drain also waits for a generation another drain is still replaying, and
returns early only with an apply error. Flush returns once every generation
is applied.
pkg/storage/writeordertest is a deterministic
model-based harness: generated programs and named schedules of direct
writes, implicit and explicit transactions held open across other steps,

* test(storage,cypher,multidb): census of stored-entity effects and their owners
testing/storagecensus builds, from the type-checked source of pkg/storage,
pkg/multidb and pkg/cypher, the census of every path that writes stored
entities, changes a count, a derived count or quota usage, takes a hidden-
entity decision next to a write, or reads an integrity or quota total, and
the owner each path goes through. A call through an interface of those
packages reaches every implementation of it there. The census is committed
as docs/generated/stored-entity-census.json and .md: sorted, with module-
relative names only, so it is the same on every toolchain, and
TestStoredEntityCensusIsCurrent fails when it is stale (regenerate with
NORNICDB_CENSUS_UPDATE=1).
TestStoredEntityEffectsPassTheirOwners enforces the owners:
- write: every path from an exported function, an exported method of an
exported type or a go statement to a physical Badger write passes a
write-order owner (a function that calls one is governed by it), or a
listed exemption;
- counter: the counted state (engine and namespace node and relationship
counts, derived counts and their deltas, a transaction's staged deltas, a
write-behind generation's count delta, a database's stored-byte usage)
changes only in a listed owner;
- hidden: a function that tests hidden or suppressed state, or reads a
stored image, and stages or performs a write itself is a listed owner;
- total: an integrity or quota total is read only by a listed reader.
Every owner belongs to a family with one reason; every exemption has its
own. Counting or total-reading state the patterns find that the spec does
not classify, and spec rows that no longer match the code, fail too.
TestOwnerGuardCatchesMutations adds each forbidden bypass to a copy of the
sources (a direct counter update, a hidden-node replace that skips the
owner, an unscoped quota read, a write that skips the write order, a go
statement that writes) and requires the census to report it. It replaces
the write-order guard that covered storage writes only.

* fix(fabric): preserve remote CALL scope and value types in v1.4.4 (#1630)
* fix(fabric): bind remote CALL imports and keep outer variables after CALL
A CALL body that runs on a remote constituent imports outer variables, but
the remote statement received the row's values only as parameters named
like the variables, so it rejected them as undefined, and the row values
replaced the caller's parameters of the same name.
Imports come from the Cypher executor's CALL subquery reader, the one its
single-database CALL execution uses, installed on the Fabric planner: the
scope clause of CALL (x) / (*) / () or the body's importing WITH (WITH x,
WITH *), read with comments as whitespace, so the result is the same with
query normalization on or off. A scope clause's variables stay visible
throughout the body: every fragment of a scoped body runs on the remote as
WITH $p AS x CALL (x) { ... } RETURN *, and the imported columns are left
out of its result. The importing-WITH form projects its imports ahead of
the body.
Every name Fabric adds to a statement (import parameters, the APPLY
pipeline's key, rows and row-wrapper names) is one that occurs nowhere in
the statement and is not a caller parameter or row variable, and no user
variable is filtered by a reserved-looking prefix. The APPLY pipeline's
row wrapper is marked on its result (ResultStream.RowWrapper) and carried
through APPLY inputs and UNION branches, never recognized by column name.
Values reach a remote participant as statement parameters, the caller's
and the imported row's alike, and the remote transport is the one owner
of how each travels (storage.RemoteParameterValue). Bolt and HTTP values
typed by the row metadata reach Fabric as one storage.RemoteTypedValue,
which the Cypher executor decodes into its temporal and point values, at
any nesting depth. A node, relationship or path is rejected with Neo4j's
invalid-import error (Neo.ClientError.Statement.TypeError, GQL status
Neo4j's HTTP API tells an integer from a float by the number's form. The
HTTP transport reads JSON numbers losslessly, in rows, nested values and
graph entities: an integer is an exact int64 and a number with a fraction
or an exponent a float64. It writes float parameters as JSON floats, so
an integral float stays a float, and a nil list or map parameter of any
type is still written as null, so SET n.p = $x removes the property. A
value relayed through an HTTP participant keeps its type and all 64 bits.
Batched correlated lookups key numbers by Cypher equality, through the
numeric equivalence keys the Cypher executor's value keys use (moved to
9007199254740992.0 do not, and NaN matches nothing, whichever transport
returned the value.
The planner recognizes CALL (x) { }, CALL (*) { } and CALL () { } with
their scope clause, so a scoped body with its own USE is planned like any
other CALL body instead of re-entering the composite in an explicit
transaction.
The rows a composite statement's leading part hands to a CALL kept only
the aliases of its last WITH, even when another clause followed it:
USE comp WITH 'ab' AS s UNWIND [1,2] AS x CALL { ... } RETURN s lost s.
A WITH now gives the leading part's columns only when it is its last
clause, its WHERE, ORDER BY, SKIP and LIMIT aside; otherwise every
variable in scope is kept.
Every temporal, spatial and duration value, a pointer to one included,
reaches a participant as its Cypher type in any parameter position, also
inside lists and maps. The Bolt transport sends each as the Neo4j Go
driver does (time.Time, dbtype.Date, ...), copying a parameter map only
when a value changes, and sends a nil pointer, list or map as null. Neo4j's
HTTP API reads parameters as plain JSON, so the HTTP transport sends such a
value, or a NaN or infinite float, as the JSON its constructor reads, and
writes each reference to that parameter as the constructor over it: an
atom valid wherever a parameter is (a map literal in CREATE (n $props), a
list comprehension for a batch of rows), whose text depends on the
values' types, not on how many rows a batch has. Time and datetime
offsets keep their seconds (+02:05:59, a historical zone's local mean
time).
A CALL scope clause item that is not a variable (CALL (1), CALL (x + 1),
CALL (x, *)), or an empty one (CALL (x,), CALL (,x), CALL (x,,y)), is
Neo4j's syntax error, reported by the scope clause reader that statement
validation, single-database execution and Fabric planning all read scope
clauses with. A scope variable the query doesn't define is Neo4j's
compile-time "Variable `x` not defined", reported where statements are
checked: a composite statement is checked as the one statement it is
without its USE clauses (FabricPlanner.SingleGraphStatement) before it
plans, enlists a participant or runs any part, and EXPLAIN and PROFILE
check the statement they plan, so the error comes before a missing
parameter and before any write. A word such as null, true, NaN or
Infinity is a variable's name there, as in Neo4j: unquoted, it imports
the variable the query binds quoted (WITH 1 AS `NaN` CALL (NaN) { ... }).

Author: Codex (R5 outcome values); rebase reconciliation and the R6/R7 owner
convergence by Claude.
Freeze operation/native truth and each child status/message at the logical
terminal owner, render the complete value through one renderer, and retain a
discarded outcome at its completion boundary (statement journal, GraphQL root
field).
One owner per behaviour:
- composition: pkg/errors/compose.Outcomes (primary first, every other cause
once); CombineTerminalOutcomes layers terminal normalization on it.
- transaction-control status: classified where the failing operation
produces it (TransactionControlFailure; NewTerminalFailure for WAL records):
a failure's own status is kept, an unclassified one takes the operation's
Neo4j 5.26 status (DatabaseError Start/Commit/RollbackFailed), a statement
abort keeps its statement's status. BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK and post-commit
failures are classified in Cypher, txsession and the Bolt lifecycle, so every
protocol and route renders the same status with the one renderer; the
consumer-side fallbacks are removed.
- transaction start: openTransaction opens every Cypher transaction, explicit
BEGIN and implicit auto-commit alike (prime, snapshot, pin, configure, WAL
begin record), and classifies its failure as a BEGIN failure.
- rendering: one pass (renderStatus) turns an error into status, message and
diagnostics, walking the error tree once; Neo4jStatus, RenderStatus,
RenderStatusWithFallback and AppendStatusDiagnostics all use it, and HTTP
renders a statement failure in one call.
- terminal outcome discovery: one error walk (statusScan) finds the first
carrier for rendering, lookupTerminalView and responseTerminalView, and
lists every carrier and enclosing primary for collectTerminalView to merge.
- MERGE retry classification: one required owner in the transaction
(cypher classifyMergeRetry). Implicit and explicit transactions on every
protocol classify their own statement and COMMIT failures before any
terminal value is frozen; the optional context classifier and Bolt's own
copy of the policy are removed. An explicit HTTP transaction's commit-time
MERGE race is now retryable as it already was over Bolt.
The decision rests on what each statement did: it observes the transaction's
commit work at its owner, including collaborators' staged dictionary state, and
only a running MERGE statement may add to it; work added at any other time
makes the failure hard. No registry, declaration or text can undo that.
A transaction holds the rule's record only once a statement can need it
(a lazy pointer; mixed transactions share one sentinel), and the context's
flags sit together, so the transaction context keeps its allocation size.
- retry classification: one owner, transientTransactionStatus; the render pass
takes its status from it and Bolt's commit-failure log severity uses
IsTransientTransactionError, the same classification without rendering.
- commit completion: explicit and implicit commits run post-commit actions,
then always write the COMMIT record; a failed record keeps the action's
failure as its primary.
- committed truth: owned by the invocation, not carried by errors. Every
native commit is published once (publishStatementCommit), which records the
committed work with the statement and every enclosing completion owner (the
statement chain terminal outcomes are recorded on, and the client
operation's TerminalOutcomeScope), whatever any child returned. When an owner
composes its returned terminal outcome (TerminalOutcomes.Retain), an
invocation that committed work adds a committed-work record. Committed truth
lives only in the record list, which every construction and composition
keeps: a view is built only by newTerminalView, which settles its status
from its records (committedStatus), and a composed outcome only by
newTerminalOutcome. The commit fact has one writer each: RecordCommit for
the journal, nextStatementOutcome for the statement state. An outcome, single
or aggregate in any child order and however constructed, never carries a
status a driver retries; a retriable one becomes
the COMMIT operation's own status (TerminalCommit.fallbackStatus). A failed
post-commit step is the committed terminal value whether or not its COMMIT
record was written. Each child keeps its own status, cause and diagnostic;
ordinary errors and healthy success are unchanged. IsRetriableStatus is the
drivers' retry decision, and Bolt's known-outcome check uses it.
The URL-sink inventory (pkg/observability testdata) classifies the 20
expressions the transaction-start owner now passes through tx/bookkeeping/err
as reviewed non-egress, and re-keys the transitionCatalog return that moved to
compose.Outcomes.
APOC function registration (merged #1685, NOR-184) composes its failures
through compose.Outcomes, the one composition owner, instead of its own
errors.Join; a cause already contained is no longer added twice.
Rebased onto release 343ca141f (#1655). Its commit-read failure
(storage.CommitFailureError) and its UNIQUE-before-conflict precedence are the
failure's own classification inside the one classification pass; the commit
status is the release's DatabaseTransactionCommitFailed (the same DatabaseError
string this change used), and the ClientError TransactionCommitFailed, whose
only producer was the removed Neo4jCommitStatus fallback, is removed. #1655's
tests use the COMMIT operation's status path. One #1655 assertion changes:
its explicit MERGE race through the Cypher executor (merge_create) expected
ConstraintValidationFailed; with the one MERGE retry decision it is
TransientOutdated, as release already reported over Bolt and for implicit
Cypher, and the case now proves the retry finds the winner's node. A public
test proves the same race is retryable, and its retry succeeds, over
embedded Cypher, Bolt and HTTP. The NOR-338 test fix now comes from the
release.

* feat(tooling): extract shared work census engine and generic controls
The engine also owns the incoming walk (WalkCallers, the reverse of
ReachableFrom over SourceCallSites), the direct population of a root
(DirectReachableFrom: static calls and literals only), the outermost enclosing
function, the in-scope context reading (ContextInScope, the reading Extract
records as a member's Scope) and a may-be-nil value flow (MayBeNil). MayBeNil
follows parameters, closures, phis, the results of every call-graph target,
and local cells and struct fields by reaching definitions (on every path the
nearest store, write that may reach the location, nil test of it or its
start). It recognizes Go's (value, error) convention when the error test lies
on every path to the use, also through an error cell, and Recover blocks that
no deferred call can enter. Each rule has must-be-silent and must-report
plants. Clients keep no private graph walk
or value-flow analysis.

* fix(storage): decide peer publication after BEGIN by one rule for buffered and replayed writes
A write reserves its MVCC version before it publishes: a direct write inside
its Badger transaction, a buffered commit at acknowledgement, before the
buffer append. A transaction that begins between the two sees the reserved
version in its boundary but not the write in its snapshot or buffer prefix,
and commit validation compared versions only, so the peer's write was taken
as seen. While the peer stayed buffered the unapplied-commit scan still
caught it; once replayed, nothing did. A stale creation then overwrote the
peer's entity and counted it twice, and a stale update or deletion counted
a removal twice or dropped an increment: the relationship-type counters
drifted above or below the stored relationships.
The engine now keeps a ledger of reserved, unpublished versions
(mvccReservations). The allocator advances the namespace sequence, fixes
the commit timestamp and enters the version in the ledger in one step under
the ledger's lock, and a transaction's cut takes its wall clock, reads its
version boundary and copies the ledger under the same lock. A version
reserved after a cut compares newer than that cut's boundary (its sequence
is higher and its timestamp is floored at the cut's clock and the
namespace's high-water mark, which the boundary is made of); one reserved
before is in the copy. Bootstrap heads keep their historical times. The cut keeps its
order, the physical snapshot and buffer prefix first and the boundary
after, so nothing in the snapshot is newer than the boundary; the ledger is
told before the snapshot, at BEGIN and at a snapshot continuation, and a
version published while a cut is in progress stays in the ledger until that
cut has its copy. snapshotHeadConflict is the one
rule for every commit path and both entity kinds: a peer head was published
after the cut when its version compares newer than the boundary, or it is
in the copy and neither the transaction's snapshot nor its buffer prefix
holds it. Buffered and replayed peers get the same answer. The copy is
nil when nothing is in flight and pooled otherwise, and the ledger keeps
its buckets, so an uncontended commit allocates what it did before.
The commit fast path that skips the head reload is now granted only to an
ID this transaction minted (CreateMintedNode, CreateMintedEdge), never by ID
shape: a caller-supplied UUID keeps the head check. The regression matrix
covers creations, updates and deletions of nodes and relationships, implicit
and explicit commits, buffered and replayed peers, plus a caller-supplied
UUID under the fast-path setting, the minted fast path itself, a frame
that removes and re-creates an identity, and a cut taken while a peer is
reserving its version.

subquery IN TRANSACTIONS or under USE, which runs its part on another
executor, and a plugin function outside the bundled APOC library, which is
